lessons.title: Understanding the farm input chain
lessons.html:
What is an input chain?

The input chain is the flow of everything the farm buys to produce: seed, fertiliser, agrochemicals, animal feed, stock remedies, fuel, packaging, spares and services such as contractors. It runs from the manufacturer through distributors and co-ops to the farm store and finally the field or animal. Inputs often make up the largest share of production costs, so managing the chain well protects both margins and timeliness.

Links in the chain

  1. Planning: what is needed, how much, when, to what specification.
  2. Sourcing: choosing suppliers on price, quality, reliability, credit terms and technical support.
  3. Purchasing: quotations, orders, contracts.
  4. Delivery and receiving: checking quantity, quality, batch numbers and expiry dates against the order.
  5. Storage: safe, legal and secure.
  6. Issuing and use: controlled issue to fields and enterprises, recorded against cost centres.
  7. Disposal of containers, waste and expired stock.

Why it fails

Common problems include late ordering before planting, stock-outs of critical spares during harvest, buying cheap but ineffective products, theft, fertiliser absorbing moisture in poor storage, expired remedies and price shocks linked to the exchange rate (many SA inputs such as fertiliser and agrochemicals are imported or priced off international markets).

Regulated inputs

Fertilisers, farm feeds, agricultural remedies and stock remedies must be registered under Act 36 of 1947. Buy only registered products with a registration number on the label, and keep proof of purchase. Seed should be certified where certification schemes apply to the crop, to guarantee purity and germination.

lessons.title: Planning, procurement and supplier management
lessons.html:
Buying the right input at the right time

Input requirement planning

Start from the production plan. For each enterprise list the area or animal numbers, the input rate and timing. For example, 200 ha of maize at a planned seeding rate and fertiliser recommendation from soil analysis gives total seed and fertiliser needs, which are then placed on a calendar showing order and delivery dates with a safety margin before planting.

Procurement decisions

  • Specification first: define what you need (cultivar, analysis, active ingredient, pack size) before comparing prices.
  • Get several quotations and compare on total cost: price, delivery, credit terms, rebates and support.
  • Timing: early ordering or pre-season contracts can lock in prices and secure supply; weigh this against storage cost and interest.
  • Group buying through study groups or co-ops can improve prices for smaller farmers.

Supplier evaluation

CriterionQuestions
QualityRegistered, certified, consistent?
ReliabilityOn time, in full?
Price and termsCompetitive, transparent, credit available?
Technical supportAgronomists, advice, after-sales service?
ComplianceLegal, ethical, proper documentation?

Score suppliers annually and keep good relationships with the best. Have a back-up supplier for critical inputs.

Controls against fraud

Separate duties: the person who orders should not be the only one who receives and approves payment. Use written orders, match invoices to delivery notes and orders before paying, and limit who may buy on the farm's account.

lessons.title: Receiving, storage and stock control
lessons.html:
Looking after inputs on the farm

Receiving

Check every delivery against the order and delivery note: product, quantity, pack condition, batch numbers and expiry dates. Reject damaged or incorrect goods and note it on the delivery note before signing.

Safe storage

  • Agrochemicals: locked, ventilated store with bunded floor to contain spills, away from water sources, food, feed and homes; warning signs; spill kit, PPE and fire extinguisher at hand. Keep products in original labelled containers.
  • Fertiliser: dry, on pallets, away from fuel and chemicals; ammonium nitrate is an oxidiser and must be kept away from combustible material.
  • Seed: cool, dry, rodent-proof; treated seed kept away from feed and people.
  • Feed and remedies: dry and vermin-free; vaccines in a monitored fridge to keep the cold chain.
  • Fuel: bunded tanks away from buildings, with no-smoking signs.

Stock control

  • Use a stock register or farm software: receipts, issues, balances.
  • Issue stock on signed requisitions linked to a field, camp or enterprise so costs are allocated correctly.
  • First expired, first out (FEFO): use the oldest stock first.
  • Do regular stock counts and investigate differences.
  • Set reorder levels for critical items like filters and belts.

Evaluating the chain

Measure input cost per hectare or per unit produced, stock-outs, wastage, supplier performance and stock losses. Compare with budgets and benchmarks, and adjust suppliers or processes.

Key points

  • Plan input needs from the production plan and order in time.
  • Buy only registered products and certified seed where applicable.
  • Compare suppliers on total value, not just price.
  • Store chemicals, fertiliser, fuel and vaccines safely and legally.
  • Use stock registers, FEFO and separation of duties to control costs and losses.
